en: The move everyone plays — guarding the bishop against g5 — and it costs dearly: the bishop has no square left and f7 collapses.
The resource: the rook lifts along the third rank, defends c3 and joins the attack. That is what playing the Blackmar-Diemer against a good defence means — seek complications, not equality.
Not Nxg6 at once: the bishop takes the long diagonal first, because without their light-squared bishop Black has nothing left to guard b7.
The bill: the a8 rook falls. That is why 8…h6 loses, and why 8…Bb4 is the move to know.
The sound defence: Black shuts the diagonal and gives material back if needed.
Ask the question immediately. Retreating to h5 lets g4 gain another tempo.
Nearly one Black player in two trades rather than retreat to h5, and the course only planned for …Bh5. They hand us the bishop pair to remove our best attacker.
The knight jumps to its outpost with tempo: there's the compensation for the pawn — active pieces, not calculations.
Know it from both sides: with accurate play Black holds, and our attack must come fast or not at all.
We play the French, and that has to be accepted: offering a gambit means accepting it can be declined. A good French beats a forced gambit.
We develop towards Black's king. The missing pawn does not come back: it buys time and open lines, so play must be fast and aimed at the king.
The brutal move, and the right one: we evict the bishop before it settles, and the g4 pawn will join the attack rather than sit at home.
We strike anyway. After the exchanges their e4 pawn becomes an isolated f-pawn and their kingside is permanently loose: the price of …f5.
The queen lands on the f-file, facing f7. The trade cost them their best minor piece AND put our queen exactly where she wanted to be.
The quiet sister of the Nimzo-Indian: when White avoids Nc3, …Bb4+ keeps the idea of controlling e4 and trading the bishop for a knight. Safe, with little heavy theory.

Without c4 there is no Bogo and no Nimzo: we play a sound position with the landmarks of an …e6 player.
The most common move — two games in three — and the course didn't mention it. The Bogo assumes 3.Nf3; here the knight goes to c3.
The Bogo check: with no Nc3 to block, White interposes on d2 and Black keeps the Nimzo spirit.
The natural block; Black will trade it at the right moment to disrupt White's coordination.
The other block: the knight goes to d2, keeping the pawn structure intact.
Support the b4 bishop and prepare …Nc6 and the …e5 break.
Prop up the b4 bishop (against a3) to keep it pinning longer.
Develop WITHOUT letting the b4 bishop go: …Nbd7 first allows Bc1 and the pin falls apart for nothing.
The same pin, but it now has another name: the Nimzo-Indian. Good news for a Bogo player — the idea is identical, only the theory differs.
The move that makes the London uncomfortable: the queen hits b2, which the bishop — gone to f4 — no longer defends.
A sound, fun gambit: give e5 back at once but get active pieces, hopping knights and very real tactical traps. Ideal at club level.

No c4, so no Budapest: …e5 would no longer be a gambit but a mistake. We develop normally and wait for c4.
Without c4 there is no Budapest: …e5 would attack nothing and drop a pawn. One White player in six plays the London, and the course only planned for c4 and Nf3.
The Budapest Gambit: offer e5 for fast development and active piece play.
More than one White player in five closes instead of taking, and the course only planned for the capture. The gambit is declined: the position becomes a closed King's Indian structure.
One White player in nine develops without committing, and the course had not planned for it. The most flexible move — and the least committal.
The knight leaps to g4: it will regain e5 and already eyes f2/e3.
The Fajarowicz: the knight jumps to e4 instead of g4, for more positional, trap-laden play.
White holds e5 with Bf4; Black pins with …Bb4+ and regains the pawn.
Nearly three White players in ten develop the knight rather than play Be2, and the course only saw Be2.
Simple development, played four times in ten, and the course only planned for Nd2. It is the reply that troubles the Fajarowicz most.
c4 came too late for the gambit — we're in a Queen's Gambit Declined, a sound and perfectly playable position.
We switch to sound play rather than force a gambit that is not there. A gambit repertoire must say what to play when the gambit is unavailable.
White avoids the bishop trade. We have what matters: a shared centre and untroubled development.
The check is our only active resource: we must develop with threats, otherwise White simply keeps the e5 pawn.
The check first: it forces White to commit, and our bishop finds an active square before the position closes around it.
We take since they did not: our centre pawn goes, but their queen has to come and collect it, and she will be chased.
King to safety before collecting the pawn. In the Budapest, hurrying costs more than the pawn itself: piece activity pays, not material.
Solidity itself: like the French, Black plays …d5 — but WITHOUT shutting in the light-squared bishop, which comes out to f5. Sound structure, clear plan.

The Two Knights: White develops quickly and keeps the central tension.
Nearly a third of games, and the course started from 2.d4. White dodges Caro-Kann theory by keeping the centre flexible.
The classical development; Black will take on e4 and free the bishop.
The Advance: the centre closes. Unlike the French, Black's bishop breathes.
The Fantasy: White props up e4 at all costs. Striking the centre is the right reaction.
The whole point of the Caro: the bishop develops BEFORE …e6. No piece shut in.
The Karpov: …Nd7 before …Ngf6, so the knight can recapture without wrecking the pawns.
The h-pawn chases the bishop to its last refuge.
Trade off White's good bishop to defuse the kingside attack.
White develops and castles long; Black will do likewise — or the other way.
A rock-solid structure; Black opts for a quiet fianchetto plan.
The bishop comes out at once — the big edge over the French.
A quarter of games after …Bf5: White offers to trade the bishop we've just developed.
Pressing on d4 and b2; Black has an easy, weakness-free game.
The Panov Attack: open play with an isolated pawn — more dynamic than the rest of the Caro.
The quiet exchange: symmetrical structure, Black equalises easily.
The punishment for 3.f3: h4 is open and the white king has nowhere to hide.
A pawn up and the white king out in the open: Black is clearly better.
Pin the f3-knight before it can prop up a White centre.
We play our move anyway. With no pawn on d4, White cannot support e4 for long.
The small trap here: after …Nxe4 the queen recaptures with a pin. Taking is still right — you just need to know what follows.
We accept without regret. The whole point of the Caro-Kann is developing this bishop BEFORE …e6; trading it for its active counterpart is a good deal.
The best of both worlds: the solid Queen's Gambit structure plus a g2 bishop raking the long diagonal. Lasting pressure, minimal risk.

Nearly a third of games, and the course started from …e6. Without …e6 there is no Catalan: Black is heading for a Grünfeld or King's Indian.
The Catalan fianchetto: the g2 bishop eyes b7 and presses permanently on d5.
One Black player in five gives this check first. It's a Bogo-Indian grafted onto our move order.
Black takes the pawn. White usually regains it thanks to the g2 bishop's pressure (Ne5, Qa4).
Keep the tension: the queen supports e4 and watches c4.
The no-nonsense recapture: the check wins c4 back at once.
We leave the Catalan plan and take the centre: the g3 fianchetto would have no target left on the long diagonal.
Pressure on d5 before Black castles — the idea that sets the tone, echoing the Catalan without sharing its structure.
Interpose the bishop rather than the knight: after the trade our bishop takes the diagonal and the fianchetto keeps its point.
Open the centre on move two. Two flavours: the Center Game (3.Qxd4, queen to e3 and aggressive long castling) or the Danish Gambit (3.c3, two pawns for lightning development and attack).

Black declines the capture and defends e5 — one player in nine, and the course only saw …exd4.
Recapture with the queen; …Nc6 gains a tempo, but the queen finds a good post on e3.
The Danish Gambit: offer one, then two pawns for blazing development and attack.
The queen tucks into e3, preparing Nc3, Bd2 and aggressive long castling.
The most common reply, and the course started elsewhere. Black frees the bishop and waits.
One game in five: Black wants …Ba6 to trade the f1 bishop and stop us castling.
The pin, played half the time here — and the course only planned for …Be7. Black targets the c3 knight to weaken e4.
Black declines the gambit and develops. One player in ten, and the course only planned for the capture …dxc3.
The clean antidote: Black GIVES the pawns back with …d5 to equalise and blunt the bishops.
The in-between check, played by nearly one Black player in three — and the course only saw …d5. They try to trade before our bishops get to work.
The bishop prepares long castling: that's the whole point of the Centre Game — otherwise the early queen sortie gains nothing.
Opposite castling. We attack with g4-h4 while they're still looking for a plan.
The knight eyes c2 and d3. Don't panic: the queen steps aside and the b4 knight ends up misplaced.
Three Black players in four develop like this after …b6, and the course only knew …Nb4. The bishop eyes our queen on e3 — which is exactly what will serve us.
We've lost castling rights; they've lost the bishop pair and two tempi. The balance favours us.
We close instead of trading: the c6 knight is pushed back, and Black ends up in a closed Ruy Lopez structure without its compensations.
The pawn hits the g6 knight before it settles. With the centre locked, a wing advance costs nothing.
We ask the question at once. If they take, our queen lands on the long diagonal and our pawns stay healthy; if they retreat, they have lost a tempo.
The queen dodges TOWARDS the attack: from g3 she eyes g7 and Black's coming castled king, and it is the bishop that must explain itself.
Castling long, the signature of the Center Game: the kings go to opposite wings, and it becomes a race of attacks in which we are a tempo ahead.
We recapture and get what the gambit was after anyway: the big centre, without having paid for it.
We block with a piece we are developing anyway. Two pawns given, two bishops trained on Black's king and full development: that is the Danish bargain, and it holds as long as we never slow down.
The anti-Tarrasch: …Nc6 at once, a game of PIECES against White's centre, even if it means giving up the bishop pair. Guaranteed imbalance, little forced theory.

One game in five, and the course started from 2.c4. The Chigorin still makes full sense here.
The Chigorin move: the knight pressures d4 first; …e5 and …Bg4 will follow.
The exchange: after …Qxd5 the queen is well placed and …e5 comes quickly.
Take on c4 to open the game for the pieces and gain time on the centre.
The pin: trade the bishop for the f3-knight to loosen White's grip on d4/e5.
Develop first; …Nc6 comes next, once the f4 bishop is already committed.
The Chigorin's core idea: pin the defender of d4 instead of building a pawn centre. Pieces before pawns.
An almost automatic setup: d4, Nf3, e3, Bd3, c3, 0-0, then the e4 break. Little theory, a clear kingside attacking plan.

Knight before pawns: Black prepares …Bg4 to trade off the defender of e5.
One Black player in six plays …e6 before developing a knight, and the course only planned for …Nf6 and …Nc6. Nothing changes for us: the Colle sets up whatever the order.
Black develops the good bishop before …e6 — the golden rule, applied here against us. One player in ten, and the course said nothing.
The system move. Modest-looking, it prepares Bd3, c3, Nbd2 and the e4 break at the right moment.
The pin before …e6: one Black player in five, and the course only saw …e6. They hamper Nf3, and so the e4 break.

We switch to the Zukertort: rather than propping up d4 with c3, the queen's bishop will rake from b2. This is the system's standard order — b3 BEFORE castling, so we never have to meet …c4 kicking the d3 bishop.
Freeing the e4 break: after …Bxc5, e4 cracks the centre and opens the attack.
The right answer: take the e5 pawn instead of retreating to d7, and the Greek gift never happens.
The Greek gift, the whole point of the Colle: the d3 bishop and f3 knight have been waiting for this since move one.
The en-passant capture reopens the lines. White has at least perpetual check — that is the system's contract.
Worth knowing: against this defence White has no attack, just a pawn less. The Colle is betting on …Nd7.
The Zukertort version: the b2 bishop rakes the long diagonal and Ne5 launches the attack.
f4 BEFORE Nd2: the other order allows …Nxe5! fxe5 Bxe5, and the d4 pawn drops for nothing.
The most common order, and the course started from 1.d4 d5. Nothing changes: the Colle is always built the same way.
Same with …e6 first: a Colle player needn't worry about it.
One Black player in four props up e5 before castling. The course started from castling, but the reverse order is common.
The announced pin. Don't just put up with it.
More than one Black player in four develops like this, and the course only knew …Bg4.
We answer with mirrored pressure on c6, and Black's pin loses its sting: their knight is hit before ours.
And not c4. This is the choice that defines the repertoire: we give up the Queen's Gambit's theoretical edge for a position we replay identically every game.
The bishop finally takes the long diagonal, the one aimed at Black's king. Without it, b3 would have been a wasted pawn move — this square is what justifies the whole system.
We offer to trade the bishop Black took care to develop. If they accept they lose their best piece; if they decline they lose time.
The break, at once: Black has spent a move on …d6 and has not castled yet. This is precisely when e4 costs the least.
The knight comes for our d3 bishop — the one that carries the whole Colle attack. A decision is needed: keeping it costs a tempo, trading doubles our pawns.
We accept the doubled pawns: the d3 pawn supports e4, the system's break. What looks like a weakness serves our plan precisely.
The bishop steps back to offer the trade on our terms: after …Bxe2 it is our queen that recaptures, and she ends up active.
With 1…f5 Black plays for the attack: control of e4 and a kingside assault. Three systems to choose from: Leningrad, Stonewall, Classical.
